The figure illustrates the architecture of MF-NeRF (Mixed-Feature Neural Radiance Fields), presented in a 2D schematic representation. The global layout is left-to-right, depicting a data processing pipeline starting from a sampled 3D point x, represented visually as a toy excavator model on a grid, progressing through a mixed-feature hash encoding module, and ending with a NeRF renderer outputting density σ and color c.

The central component is the 'Mixed-feature hash encoding' block, enclosed in a dashed rectangle. This block contains two parallel processing streams corresponding to different grid resolutions: one for grid GL (higher resolution, shown with orange grid lines) and another for grid GL−1 (lower resolution, shown with blue grid lines). Each grid contains a small 3D model (the excavator) overlaid on a grid structure. For each grid, an index transformation operation, labeled 'Index_trans_{G_L}(I^{g_L})' for GL and 'Index_trans_{G_{L-1}}(I^{g_{L-1}})' for GL−1, maps the indices of the current grid to those of the highest-resolution grid GL. This transformation ensures that both grids can reference the same hash table entries for spatially congruent coordinates, as demonstrated by the red dots at the lower-right corners of corresponding voxels in the orange and blue grids.

Following the index transformations, feature vectors f_L and f_{L−1} are computed for each grid. These are visualized as small neural network-like diagrams with circular nodes connected by edges; f_L is shown in orange and f_{L−1} in blue. The outputs of these networks are fed into a shared 'MF hash table for G_{L−1} and G_L', which is depicted as a vertical stack of rectangular bins. The hash function h(I^{g_L}) maps the transformed indices to specific bins in this table. The feature vectors from different levels are stored in distinct colored regions within the hash table—orange for f_L and blue for f_{L−1}, with intermediate levels implied by the ellipsis.

The final step in the encoding stage is the concatenation of all feature vectors from level 1 to L, denoted by ⊕ (explicitly defined as 'concatenation' in the figure's legend). This concatenated vector y is then passed to the 'NeRF Renderer', shown as a gray box with green vertical bars on either side, symbolizing a multi-layer perceptron or similar network. The renderer also receives the positional embedding of the viewing direction γ(d) as input. The output of the renderer is the density σ and color c for the sampled point x.

The figure uses color coding consistently: orange for higher-resolution components (GL), blue for lower-resolution components (GL−1), and gray for the renderer. Text labels are placed near relevant components, and arrows indicate the flow of data. The overall design emphasizes the hierarchical and shared nature of the hash encoding, enabling efficient feature reuse across scales.

The figure presents a hardware architecture for convolution operations, emphasizing runtime configurability and modular design. The global layout is horizontal, depicting a dataflow pipeline from left to right, with distinct functional blocks grouped into larger subsystems. A vertical red line divides the diagram into two main stages: the input/data preparation stage on the left and the computation/accumulation stage on the right. Another vertical red line further marks the boundary between the computation and output accumulation phases.

On the far left, a 'Sliding Window' block contains three 'Line Buffer' modules, each represented as a light blue rectangle with a cross-hatch pattern, indicating they are compile-time configurable but can be bypassed at runtime. These buffers receive input data streams and feed them into a central 'Broadcast' module, shown as a tall red trapezoid, which is runtime configurable. This Broadcast unit routes data to two parallel processing paths.

Each path includes a 'Crossbar' module—also red and runtime configurable—which directs data to a set of DSP (Digital Signal Processing) units. The top path has three DSPs feeding into an 'Adder Tree' within a 'Vector Dot' block; the bottom path mirrors this structure. The Adder Trees are depicted as large light blue triangles, representing compile-time configurable hardware. Each path's output is summed via a circular '+' symbol (accumulator) and stored in an 'Accumulator Buffer', a light blue rectangle with cross-hatching, again indicating compile-time configurability with runtime bypass capability.

A 'Parameter Controller' block, colored red and positioned at the top-left, sends dashed lines to both Crossbars and the Broadcast unit, signifying runtime control signals that dynamically configure these components. The dashed lines imply non-data, control-path communication.

The legend at the bottom-left clarifies the color coding: red blocks are runtime configurable, light blue are compile-time configurable, and cross-hatched elements denote hardware that can be bypassed at runtime. The overall workflow shows how input data is buffered, broadcast, routed through configurable crossbars, processed by DSPs and adder trees, accumulated, and stored, all under dynamic control from the Parameter Controller. The architecture supports flexible, runtime-adaptive convolution computations by enabling selective activation or bypassing of hardware modules.

The figure illustrates a testing pipeline divided into three main stages: Seed Generation, Scheduling, and Testing Stage, each enclosed in a dashed rectangular box with a gray header. The overall layout is horizontal, progressing from left to right, representing a sequential workflow.

The figure presents two main architectural components: the Text-driven Appearance Discriminator (TAD) on the left and the Collaborative Attention Module (CAM) on the right. The TAD is structured into three primary parts: multi-modal based semantic supervision, a standard discriminator network, and a high-pass filter branch. The multi-modal supervision block, enclosed in a light blue dashed box, contains an Image Encoder (labeled Enc_i, peach-colored trapezoid with a lock icon) and a Text Encoder (labeled Enc_t, same style), which process an input image I and corresponding text descriptions ("low light image" T_L and "high light image" T_H, respectively). These encoders output feature vectors (yellow and purple bars) that are compared via Cosine Similarity, visualized as a 3D plot showing points A and B with angle θ and distance dist(A,B), forming a semantic alignment mechanism. Below this, the main Discriminator network (light purple background) consists of a sequence of Conv layers (teal), Instance Normalization (IN, yellow), and Leaky ReLU activation (white) blocks, culminating in a Real/Fake classification output. A separate branch applies a High-pass Filter to the input image I, producing a high-frequency version (shown as a grayscale, edge-enhanced image), which is then fed into another Discriminator instance. The CAM, shown on the right in a light peach background, processes features from the main network. It begins with AvgPool and MaxPool operations (yellow boxes) whose outputs are concatenated (C symbol) and passed through a Fully Connected Layer (FC, gray), ReLU, and another FC layer. This generates a channel-wise attention map (represented as a horizontal bar with color gradients). The attention map is multiplied (× symbol) with the original features, and the result is further processed by another AvgPool/MaxPool → Concat → Conv → ReLU pipeline. The legend at the bottom clarifies symbols: × denotes multiplication, C denotes concatenation, FC is a fully connected layer, IN is instance normalization, and yellow/purple bars represent feature vectors. The overall layout positions the TAD on the left, with the CAM on the right, and the flow is indicated by arrows connecting components, emphasizing the dual-path discrimination and attention refinement strategy.

The figure is divided into four main panels labeled (a) through (d), illustrating a comparative methodology for graph-based self-supervised learning, with a focus on masked graph reconstruction and self-supervision strategies.

Panel (a), titled 'Masked graph', displays a small undirected graph with eight nodes. Nodes 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, and 8 are represented as blue-filled circles or squares, indicating they are visible. Nodes 3 and 4 are shown as gray-outlined circles, indicating they are masked. Solid black lines represent connections between nodes. A dashed line with a red question mark connects node 1 to node 4, symbolizing an unknown or missing edge to be predicted.

Panel (b), titled 'Bipartite graph', shows two sets of graphs enclosed in light peach and light green ovals, representing two complementary views. The left set contains multiple instances of a graph (labeled x_i^v, x_{i+1}^v, etc.), where some nodes are visible (blue) and others are masked (gray). The right set contains a single instance (labeled x_j^m) with similar node types. These views are connected by a large curved arrow, suggesting a transformation or correspondence between them, forming a bipartite structure.

Panels (c) and (d) compare two self-supervision approaches. Both show a bipartite structure with three columns: 'Visible' (left, light peach oval), 'Masked' (middle, light green oval), and 'Exp.-SS' (right, no background). In both, visible nodes (blue circles/squares) are connected via solid lines to masked nodes (gray circles/squares), which are then matched via bidirectional arrows to their corresponding nodes in the 'Exp.-SS' column (blue circles/squares). This represents explicit self-supervision (Exp.-SS).

In panel (c), 'GraphMAE', the matching is direct and only involves explicit supervision. In panel (d), 'RARE (ours)', an additional dashed arrow points from the predicted node 4 in the 'Exp.-SS' column back to the masked node 4 in the middle column, labeled 'Imp.-SS' (implicit self-supervision). This indicates that RARE leverages high-order sample correlations as implicit supervision signals, which are not directly observable from raw data.

A legend at the bottom defines the visual elements: white circle = Category 1, white square = Category 2, gray-outlined circle/square = Masked node, blue-filled circle/square = Visible node, bidirectional arrow = Node matching, solid line = Node connection. The overall layout is structured to first present the problem (masked graph), then the data structure (bipartite graph), followed by a side-by-side comparison of two methods, highlighting the innovation of RARE in incorporating implicit self-supervision.

The figure presents the overall framework of S2T, divided into two main phases: Train Process and Test Process, separated by a vertical line. The layout is horizontally structured, with the left side dedicated to training and the right to testing, each containing a graph representation, feature processing modules, and downstream components.

In the Train Process section, on the left, a graph is shown with nodes in various colors: purple, orange, blue, and one red node labeled 'S' at the center. The graph includes two nested neighborhoods: an inner dashed blue box labeled 'N₁' enclosing the red node and its immediate neighbors, and an outer orange-dashed box labeled 'N_h' encompassing a broader set of nodes. From this graph, 'Node Features' are extracted and fed into a stack of GNN layers—specifically, a 'GNN 1-Layer' followed by a 'GNN h-Layer', depicted as light orange rounded rectangles with downward-pointing arrows indicating sequential processing. A separate 'Global Information' module, shown as a purple rounded rectangle, connects to the GNN stack and contributes to the computation of 'Structural Intensity', represented as a gray rectangular output box.

Parallel to the structural path, a 'Temporal Information Modeling' block is shown below the GNN stack. It contains a small graph illustrating a sequence of events around the red node 'S' at timestamps t₁, t₂, and t₃, forming a circular timeline. Adjacent to this is a bar chart titled 'Time Closer, Weight Higher', where the height of bars at t₁, t₂, and t₃ increases with proximity to the current time, visually representing the weight assigned to temporal events. All modules are enclosed in light gray rounded rectangles with soft shadows, giving a layered, modular appearance. Text labels are clear and positioned near their respective components. The figure illustrates the architecture of a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) designed to generate a bird’s-eye view (BEV) representation from multi-modal inputs. The overall layout is divided into two main vertical streams: the Generator on the left and the Discriminator on the right, with shared components indicated at the bottom. The Generator processes inputs including 'trajectory' (1x192x192), 'rgb' (9x192x192), and 'birdview' (3x192x192), while the Discriminator receives 'command' (4 one-hot, 5 traj_points(x,y), 14). These inputs feed into respective encoder-like structures composed of convolutional layers.

The Generator begins with a series of 4x4 Convolutional layers with stride 2, progressively reducing spatial dimensions while increasing channel depth: starting from 64 channels (64x95x95), then 128 (128x46x46), 256 (256x22x22), and again 256 (256x10x10). Each layer uses LeakyReLU activation and Instance Normalization (IN), except the fourth layer which includes a 0.5 Dropout. The network then transitions into a decoder phase using transposed convolutions (ConvT): 256→128→64→128→3 channels, with padding applied to maintain spatial consistency. The final output is a 3x192x192 BEV image. Skip connections link corresponding encoder and decoder layers, forming a U-Net structure.

The Discriminator starts with a 64-dimensional fully connected (FC) layer with bias and ReLU activation, followed by 4x4 Conv layers with stride 2: 128 channels (128x4x4), then 128 channels again (128x10x10). This output is padded to 384x11x11 before being fed into a 4x4 Conv layer with 1 channel and 1x1x1 padding, producing a 1x1x10 feature map. This is followed by 'Discriminator layers', which are not detailed in the diagram but implied to be further processing steps.

Shared components are labeled as 'Common layers', suggesting modular reuse between Generator and Discriminator, though the figure does not show explicit parameter sharing. The diagram uses color-coding: orange for input and Generator layers, blue for Discriminator-specific layers, and gray for shared or intermediate layers. Text within each box specifies layer type, kernel size, stride, number of filters, normalization, activation, and output dimensions. Arrows indicate data flow: inputs enter top layers, propagate downward through encoders, and then either decode (Generator) or continue to classification (Discriminator). A horizontal arrow connects the Discriminator’s 128x10x10 output to the Generator’s 256x10x10 layer via a pad operation, indicating conditional input fusion. The caption clarifies that this is a conditional GAN where Generator translates RGB and trajectory inputs to BEV, and the two networks are separate with no shared parameters.

The figure presents an overview of MSQNet, a multi-modal multi-label action recognition framework, structured into four main stages: Input, Encoder, Decoder, and Output, as indicated by the horizontal color-coded bar at the bottom. The global layout is left-to-right, depicting a data flow from raw inputs to final classification logits.

On the left, under 'Input', video frames (labeled I₁ to Iₖ) are shown as a sequence of images, representing temporal video data. Below this, a list of multiclass labels—'Eating', 'Keeping', 'Jumping', 'Standing'—is provided, each with distinct colors (green, red, cyan, olive), indicating potential action classes for prediction.

The 'Encoder' stage begins with two parallel pathways. The top pathway processes video frames through a 'Video Encoder' (light green rounded rectangle with a flame icon, indicating learnable parameters). This module outputs C×512 dimensional features, which are passed to a 'Global Encoder' (light blue rounded rectangle, also with a flame icon). The Global Encoder feeds into the 'Multi-Modal Transformer Decoder'.

The bottom pathway involves vision-language processing. Video frames are also fed into a 'CLIP Image Encoder' (bright cyan rounded rectangle with a snowflake icon, denoting frozen modules). Its output is projected via a 'Project' block (orange rectangle) into K×512 dimensional features. Simultaneously, the multiclass labels are encoded using a 'CLIP Text Encoder' (light yellow rounded rectangle with a snowflake icon), producing 'Learnable Label Embeddings' (yellow rectangle with colored bars, labeled K×512, and marked with a flame icon). These embeddings pass through an 'MLP' (light green rectangle with a flame icon) before being combined with the projected image features in a 'Multi-Modal Fusion' step. The result is a set of 'Multi-Modal Query' tokens (pink vertical bars in a white box), which are fed into the decoder.

The 'Decoder' stage consists of a 'Multi-Modal Transformer Decoder' (lavender rounded rectangle with a flame icon), which receives both the global video features and the multi-modal queries. The decoder's output is processed by a 'FFN' (feed-forward network, light green rectangle with a flame icon), leading to the 'Output' stage.

In the 'Output' section, a bracketed list displays 'Logits' for each action class: Eating (0.15), Keeping (0.45), Jumping (0.05), Standing (0.35), indicating predicted probabilities for multi-label classification.

Connections are represented by solid black arrows showing data flow. Dashed lines indicate optional or auxiliary connections, such as the dotted line from video frames to the CLIP Image Encoder. A legend in the bottom right clarifies that snowflake icons denote frozen modules (fixed weights) and flame icons denote learnable parameters (trained during optimization). The overall design emphasizes a dual-encoder architecture combining spatio-temporal video features with vision-language alignment for robust multi-label action recognition.

The figure illustrates the architectural flow of a Vision Transformer (ViT) model, emphasizing the replacement of the standard Pointwise Feedforward (PFF) layer with a proposed LIFE module to enhance local context integration within the multi-head self-attention mechanism. The global layout is left-to-right, beginning with an input image divided into N non-overlapping patches, each represented as a blue square. These patches are processed through a 'Patch Embedding' module, depicted as a gray rectangular block, which converts each patch into a token representation. A legend at the top-left indicates that yellow squares represent Class Tokens, blue squares represent Patch Tokens, and brown squares represent Position Embeddings. Each patch token is concatenated with a position embedding (brown), forming an embedded token sequence. A special Class Token (yellow) is prepended to this sequence before entering the Transformer encoder stack.

The core of the architecture consists of L stacked Transformer blocks, enclosed within a large light-gray box labeled 'Transformer Block xL'. Within each block, the embedded tokens first pass through a green rounded rectangle labeled 'PFF Layer or LIFE Module', indicating the modular design where the standard PFF layer can be replaced by the proposed LIFE module. From this module, three outputs are generated: Query Q, Key K, and Value V, shown as white rounded rectangles with black borders. These are fed into a blue vertical rectangle labeled 'Multi-head Self Attention', which computes attention scores across all tokens. The output of the attention mechanism is added to the original input via a gray 'Add' block, implementing residual connections. This summed output then passes through a blue vertical rectangle labeled 'MLP' (Multilayer Perceptron), followed by another gray 'Add' block for residual connection, completing one Transformer block. This entire block structure is repeated L times.

After processing through all L blocks, the final sequence of tokens is passed to a 'Classification Head', represented as a tall gray rectangle. The Class Token (yellow), which has been updated throughout the Transformer blocks, is extracted from the token sequence and fed into the Classification Head. The head produces the final 'Predictions', indicated by a rightward arrow leading to the label 'Predictions'. The remaining patch tokens (blue) are not used for classification but are shown as trailing dots to indicate their presence in the output sequence. The diagram uses solid blue arrows to denote data flow, with clear directional connections between modules. The visual design employs distinct colors and shapes to differentiate components: green for the customizable module, blue for attention and MLP layers, gray for embedding, addition, and classification components, and white for intermediate query/key/value representations. The overall structure reflects a standard ViT pipeline with a key modification in the internal block design to improve local feature modeling.

The figure presents an end-to-end differentiable framework for human pose estimation using an Inverse Kinematics Optimization Layer (IKOL). The global layout is divided into two main branches: the Regression Branch on the left and the Optimization Branch on the right, connected by a forward pass and backpropagation paths indicated by solid, dashed, and dotted arrows. The entire process begins with an input image showing a person in motion, specifically a baseball pitcher, highlighted with a red bounding box. This image is fed into a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), depicted as a blue trapezoid, which regresses three key components: 3D joint positions P (shown as a 3D scatter plot with a skeletal path), a rest pose T (represented as a full-body 3D human model with arms outstretched), and a twist angle φ (illustrated as a hand with a wrist twist). These outputs are grouped under a large curly brace labeled {T, P, φ}. A solid black arrow indicates the forward pass from the CNN to these outputs. From this group, a solid black arrow leads to the Optimization Branch, which contains the 'Inverse Kinematics Optimization Layer' — a light green rounded rectangle containing the mathematical expression: α* = arg min ||P - f(α; T, φ)|| over α ∈ R^23. This layer computes the optimal joint angles α* that minimize the difference between predicted 3D joints and those generated by a forward kinematic function f. The output α* is shown as a 3D human model in a crouched pitching pose. Below the optimization layer, a sequence of images illustrates the iterative optimization process, showing progressive refinements from α₁ to αₖ, each superimposed on the original input image. These iterations are connected by solid black arrows. A red dashed arrow from αₖ points downward to a beige rounded rectangle labeled 'Gauss-Newton Differentiation', which contains the equation: ∂αₖ/∂P = ∂αₖ₋₁/∂P - (∂H(αₖ₋₁,P)/∂P) ΔPₖ₋₁ - H(αₖ₋₁,P) (∂Pₖ₋₁/∂P). This module enables backpropagation through the optimization process. A red dashed arrow from this module loops back to the regression branch, indicating the gradient flow for the optimization loss L_opt, which is shown as a red dashed arrow pointing leftward above the optimization branch. Similarly, a yellow dashed arrow labeled 'Regression Loss L_reg' points leftward above the regression branch, indicating the backward pass for the regression loss. A legend at the bottom left clarifies the arrow types: solid black for forward pass, yellow dashed for regression loss, and red dashed for optimization loss. The entire framework is designed to be trained end-to-end using Gauss-Newton Differentiation (GN-Diff) to compute gradients through the optimization layer.

The figure presents a schematic diagram of the DeepONet architecture, which is designed to approximate solution operators for parametric partial differential equations. The global layout is horizontally oriented, depicting a two-branch computational pipeline that converges into a final output through element-wise multiplication operations. On the left side, two distinct input streams are shown: one for functional inputs and another for spatial coordinate inputs. The top stream receives two sets of function evaluations—β(x₁), ..., β(xₙ) and Hⁿ(x₁), ..., Hⁿ(xₙ)—which are collected within dashed rectangular boxes outlined in blue. These represent evaluations of the functions β and Hⁿ at N fixed sensor points xᵢ ∈ ℳ. This entire functional input block feeds into a 'Branch net', represented as a solid blue rectangle. The Branch net processes these inputs and produces a 2p-dimensional feature embedding vector b, partitioned into two p-dimensional segments: b₁ to bₚ (highlighted in yellow) and bₚ₊₁ to b₂ₚ (highlighted in cyan). The bottom stream receives the continuous coordinate input x = (x, y), depicted as a black arrow pointing to a 'Trunk net'—a solid red rectangle. The Trunk net outputs another 2p-dimensional embedding vector t, similarly divided into t₁ to tₚ (yellow) and tₚ₊₁ to t₂ₚ (cyan). The two embedding vectors b and t are then combined via element-wise multiplication (denoted by circular nodes with × symbols). Specifically, the first half of b (b₁ to bₚ) multiplies with the second half of t (tₚ₊₁ to t₂ₚ), producing an intermediate output labeled G_θ^x(β, Hⁿ)(x). The figure illustrates a method for adapting the CLIP model to understand social dynamics in natural dyadic conversations by leveraging GPT-3-generated responses under different listener goals. At the top, a natural dyadic conversation is depicted with a speaker saying, 'I studied very hard but I still failed my machine learning exam,' and a listener observing. The speaker’s transcript feeds into two parallel GPT-3 models, each conditioned on a different listener goal: one on the observed goal ('be social') and the other on a counterfactual goal ('not be social'). The GPT-3 model conditioned on 'be social' generates a response described as 'sympathetic and concerned,' while the one conditioned on 'not be social' generates 'amused with a large grin.' These generated responses are then processed through separate CLIP Text Encoders, which project them into an embedding space. In this embedding space, the representation of the socially correct response (from the 'be social' path) is pulled closer to a target point (indicated by a green arrow labeled 'Pull Together'), while the representation of the socially incorrect response (from the 'not be social' path) is pushed away (indicated by a red arrow labeled 'Push Apart'). This target point is derived from the CLIP Vision Encoder, which processes a learned visual prompt extracted from the listener's image. The learned visual prompt is trained using a contrastive loss to align the visually grounded listener representation with the socially appropriate textual response and to disassociate it from the inappropriate one. The overall structure is modular, with distinct components for text generation (GPT-3), text encoding (CLIP Text Encoder), vision encoding (CLIP Vision Encoder), and embedding manipulation (embedding space with push/pull operations). The diagram uses color-coded boxes: orange for the counterfactual goal, green for the observed goal, blue for the GPT-3 and CLIP encoders, and yellow for the learned visual prompt. Arrows indicate data flow and transformation, with dashed lines connecting the listener image to the observed goal and solid lines showing the main processing pipeline. The figure emphasizes the use of GPT-3 to generate synthetic negative examples (counterfactual responses) to address the scarcity of negative pairs in real video data, enabling effective contrastive training for social behavior understanding.

The figure illustrates the architecture of the MSIL (Multi-Scale Integrated Learning) network, designed for object detection tasks. The global layout is divided into three main components: Backbone, FPN (Feature Pyramid Network), and Head, arranged horizontally from left to right. The Backbone consists of stacked blue parallelograms representing convolutional layers, which extract hierarchical features. These features are then fed into the FPN, depicted as green parallelograms arranged in a pyramid structure with lateral connections (green arrows) and top-down paths (black arrows), enabling multi-scale feature fusion. Each level of the FPN connects to a separate 'head' module, shown as beige rectangles labeled 'head', indicating parallel processing for different scales.

The Head component is expanded in a large dashed blue rectangle on the right, showing its internal structure in detail. This section is further subdivided into three vertical zones: Semantic alignment (light purple), Semantic fusion (light green), and Semantic separation (light pink). In the Semantic alignment stage, two identical Shared Encoder modules (light blue rectangles labeled 'Shared Encoder') process features from the classification and regression branches, denoted as f_enc and f_enc2. These encoders receive inputs from Conv layers (blue and gray rectangles) and perform element-wise addition (indicated by ⊕ symbols) with their respective input features to produce aligned features: F_cls-align and F_reg-align.

In the Semantic fusion stage, these aligned features are concatenated (indicated by ○ symbol) and passed through a Conv layer to generate fused features, labeled f_fusion. This stage is visually represented by a light green background and a central Conv block.

The Semantic separation stage, highlighted in light pink, processes the fused features using two distinct Channel Attention Modules (CAMs, black rectangles with rounded corners). Each CAM is connected to a separate Decoder (blue and gray rectangles labeled 'Decoder'), producing outputs f_dec and f'_dec. These decoder outputs are then combined via element-wise multiplication (indicated by ⊙ symbol) with the corresponding branch features before being passed through final Conv layers to output class predictions and bounding box coordinates, respectively.

The figure includes a legend at the bottom explaining the symbols: ⊕ denotes element-wise addition, ○ denotes concatenation, and ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication. The overall flow follows a clear progression from backbone feature extraction, through FPN multi-scale enhancement, to head-level semantic alignment, fusion, and separation for final prediction. The design emphasizes shared encoding, cross-branch feature alignment, and subsequent semantic disentanglement to improve detection accuracy.

The figure presents a two-part architectural diagram illustrating both the training and inference phases of a composed image retrieval system using a learned mapping network. The left side, titled 'Training Mapping Network with Image-Only', shows the training setup. It begins with an input image (e.g., a cat photo) fed into a frozen Visual Encoder (light blue trapezoid), producing a visual feature vector v. Simultaneously, a text prompt ('A photo of') is tokenized into embeddings, represented as a sequence of light yellow boxes labeled 'A', 'photo', 'of', followed by a special pseudo-word token s (a light yellow box). This tokenized sequence is processed by a frozen Text Encoder (light yellow trapezoid), generating a text feature vector p. A trainable mapping network f_M (orange parallelogram) takes the visual feature v as input and outputs a modified representation that is aligned with the text feature p. The alignment is enforced via a contrastive loss computed between v and p, which backpropagates through f_M to optimize it. The visual and text encoders remain fixed during this process.

The right side, titled 'Composed Image Retrieval', illustrates the inference phase. An input image (e.g., a dog) is passed through the same frozen Visual Encoder, producing a feature vector. This feature is then fed into the trained mapping network f_M, which generates a query feature. Concurrently, a partial text prompt ('in pool') is tokenized and processed by the frozen Text Encoder to produce another part of the query feature. These two features are combined to form a complete query feature. This query is then used to search within a database of candidate images, each encoded by the same Visual Encoder into a set of features (represented as a circle containing blue dots and triangles). The system retrieves the most similar image based on feature similarity, shown as a dog swimming in a pool. The diagram includes explicit labels such as 'Query feature', 'Search an image', and 'Retrieved Image' to clarify the flow. The overall layout is split vertically into training (left) and inference (right) components, with consistent color-coding: light blue for visual encoders, light yellow for text encoders, and orange for the mapping network f_M. All connections are directed arrows indicating data flow, with the contrastive loss forming a feedback loop during training.

The figure illustrates the architecture of the C-T2I (Conditional Text-to-Image) component, which performs a single denoising step to generate an image from a noisy input, conditioned on multiple guidance modalities: a textual prompt, a sketch, and object bounding boxes with associated text descriptions. The core of the architecture is enclosed within a dashed rectangular boundary labeled 'C-T2I'. Inside this module, the noisy image Z_t first passes through a ResBlock (light gray rounded rectangle), followed by an Aug Self-Att block (light green rounded rectangle), then an Add operation (light gray rounded rectangle). The output of the Add block feeds into a Cross-Attention (Cross-Att) module (light blue rounded rectangle), which contains query (Q), key (K), and value (V) components, along with attention matrices A_Q, B_Q, A_K, B_K, A_V, B_V, indicating the use of augmented attention mechanisms. Connections and arrows indicate the flow of information: the prompt and sketch embeddings are merged and sent to both the Cross-Att module and the Unet Block. Additionally, the bounding box-text embeddings are routed directly to the Unet Block. The output of the Cross-Att module connects to the Unet Block, completing the forward pass. The figure also includes annotations such as 'embedding' above the prompt-to-E_T connection, and '<box, text>' below the bounding box inputs, emphasizing the multi-modal conditioning strategy. The caption notes that LoRA is used to learn personalized weights in self- and cross-attention layers and to assign specific tokens for each character, ensuring identity consistency during generation.

The likelihood update computes weights for particles based on sensor observations, while the resampling step redistributes particles according to these weights. This module is connected to a 'Dynamical model' (blue border, light blue fill) via a solid black arrow labeled 'PF', indicating the particle filter's propagation of state estimates over time. The figure presents an overview of a multimodal classification framework, referred to as \methodNick, which integrates visual and textual information for category prediction. These candidate categories are then processed by a fine-tuned VLM (denoted ftVLM, shown as an orange trapezoid), producing a set of text-based embeddings represented as orange crosses in a latent space.

The figure presents an overview of the comparative loss framework, structured vertically to illustrate the data flow from input to final loss computation. At the bottom, the 'Input Context x' is shown as a pink rectangular box, feeding into a series of neural network models represented by blue outlined diagrams with interconnected nodes. These models are labeled as f(x^(0); θ^(0)), f(x^(1); θ^(1)), ..., f(x^(c); θ^(c)), indicating different model configurations or states. Above the models, the 'Predictions' layer displays bar charts labeled y^(0), y^(1), ..., y^(c), representing the outputs of each model configuration. These predictions feed upward into a central yellow rectangular box labeled 'Task-specific Loss Function L(y, ŷ)', which computes individual task-specific losses l^(0), l^(1), ..., l^(c) for each prediction against the true label y. The 'Output Label y' is shown on the left as a light green box, connected via a gray arrow to the loss function, indicating it serves as ground truth.

The next layer, 'Loss Differences', shows a series of circular nodes with a minus sign inside, representing pairwise comparisons between adjacent losses. These are connected by colored lines: green for l^(0) to l^(1), brown for l^(1) to l^(2), etc., up to red for l^(c) to l^(c+1). Each comparison node outputs a difference signal, which is then fed into a set of circular nodes with a hinge symbol, labeled 'Hinge loss' in the legend, indicating the application of a hinge loss function to enforce ordering constraints between successive losses.

At the top, these hinge loss outputs converge into a large circular node with a sigma symbol (Σ), labeled 'Sum', which aggregates them into the final comparative loss, denoted as ℒ_cmp(x, y; θ). This final loss is positioned at the apex of the diagram, summarizing the entire comparative process.

On the right side, a legend clarifies the symbols: the sigma circle represents 'Sum', the circle with a minus sign represents 'Hinge loss', and the red scissors represent 'Ablate neurons'. The vertical axis on the left labels the layers: Input Context x, Predictions, Output Label y, Task-specific Losses, Loss Differences, and Comparative Loss, guiding the viewer through the hierarchical structure. The diagram uses distinct colors—pink for input, blue for models, green/brown/red for loss paths—to differentiate components and emphasize the progression from intact to ablated models and the resulting loss comparisons.

The figure illustrates the architecture of a deep learning-based image denoising model, designed to reconstruct a clean image x from a noisy input y. The overall layout is a left-to-right flow, starting with the noisy image on the far left and ending with the denoised image on the far right. The central processing pipeline is divided into two main sub-networks: an upper sub-network F₃ and a lower sub-network F₄, which are connected via a shared feature extraction module called SCAM (Spatial Channel Attention Module). 

The process begins with the noisy image y being fed into a Noise Estimation Network, represented as a light pink rounded rectangle. This network outputs a noise estimate, which is then concatenated (denoted by ⊕ symbol) with the original noisy image to form feature map F₁. This concatenated feature is passed through a yellow rectangular block representing a convolutional layer, leading to the SCAM module, depicted as a green cube. The SCAM processes the features and outputs feature map F₂, which serves as the input to both the upper and lower sub-networks.

The upper sub-network F₃, enclosed in a dashed brown border, consists of a series of yellow rectangular blocks representing standard convolutional layers arranged in an encoder-decoder structure. The encoder part involves downsampling operations (indicated by red arrows pointing downward), while the decoder part involves upsampling (indicated by blue arrows pointing upward). Red short skip connections link corresponding layers within the encoder and decoder, facilitating gradient flow and preserving spatial information. A long skip connection (blue arrow) connects the first layer of the encoder to the last layer of the decoder, enabling direct transmission of low-level features.

The lower sub-network F₄, enclosed in a dashed blue border, comprises a sequence of blue rectangular blocks representing dilated convolutional layers. These layers are connected by multiple red short skip connections that span across several layers, allowing the network to capture multi-scale contextual information without reducing spatial resolution. The output features from both sub-networks are combined using element-wise addition (⊕) and concatenation (⊙) operations before being passed through a final convolutional layer (yellow block) to produce the denoised image x.

The legend at the bottom left clarifies the visual elements: red arrows denote short skip connections, blue arrows denote long skip connections, yellow rectangles represent convolutional layers, and blue rectangles represent dilated convolutional layers. The symbols ⊕ and ⊙ indicate element-wise addition and concatenation, respectively. The entire architecture is framed by a blue border, emphasizing the end-to-end nature of the model.

The figure illustrates the architecture of a method called C-DECOMPOSER and C-COMPRESSOR, designed for processing event tensor streams in a time-evolving manner. The global layout is divided into three horizontal sections: the top section represents the input event tensor streams, the middle section details the C-DECOMPOSER module, and the bottom section describes the C-COMPRESSOR module.

In the top section, the input is a 3D tensor labeled 'Event tensor streams: X', extending along the time axis t from left to right. The tensor has dimensions U1 (height), U2 (width), and T (time). A sliding window of length τ is shown at the end of the tensor, denoted as XC, which is the current input segment being processed. This segment contains sparse event data represented by gray and blue dots, with blue dots indicating recent events within the window.

The middle section, labeled 'C-DECOMPOSER', processes the current segment XC. It receives input from the past L candidate regimes, shown as a sequence of dashed and solid 3D blocks representing previous regime states. These are collectively labeled as 'Set of past L candidate regimes: Q'. The C-DECOMPOSER uses these past regimes to generate a new candidate regime θc, depicted as a 2D block with two red rectangular components: A(1) aligned with U1, and A(2) aligned with U2, along with a horizontal component B of length K, oriented along τ. The candidate regime is shown in a gray box, with arrows indicating its derivation from the past regimes.

The bottom section, labeled 'C-COMPRESSOR', handles the assignment and storage of regimes. It begins with a definition: 'Regime θ = {{A(m)}m=1,M, B}', indicating that each regime consists of M components A(m) and one component B. A stack of colored blocks (blue, orange, green, red) represents different regimes θ1, θ2, ..., θR+1, with each regime composed of A(1), A(2), and B components. These are grouped under a curly brace and connected to a cylindrical database labeled 'Regime set Θ'.

The C-COMPRESSOR also includes a timeline of colored cubes below, representing regime assignments S over time. Each cube corresponds to a time step and is color-coded to indicate which regime is active. The colors match those in the regime stack, showing the temporal evolution of regime usage. The last cube, at time T, is red, corresponding to the newly generated candidate regime θc. An arrow from the Regime set Θ points to the final red cube, indicating that if the candidate regime is selected, it is added to the set as θR+1. Additionally, an output arrow from the Regime set leads to 'score(XC)', signifying the computation of an anomalousness score for the current tensor segment XC based on the selected regime.

Connections between modules are shown via black arrows: from XC to the C-DECOMPOSER, from the past regimes Q to the candidate regime θc, from θc to the Regime set Θ, and from Θ to both the regime assignment timeline and the score output. The entire process reflects a sequential, time-dependent regime decomposition and compression pipeline, where past regimes inform the generation of a new candidate, which is then evaluated and potentially stored for future use.

The figure presents an overview of the Multi-Scale Projector (MSP) module, which is designed to extract style codes from an input image I. The global layout is divided into two main sections by dashed borders: the left section, enclosed in a yellow dashed box, represents the MSP module itself, while the right section, enclosed in an orange dashed box, details the internal structure of the Style projector.

In the MSP module on the left, the input image I, symbolized by a blue-bordered icon with a stylized 'H' shape, is processed sequentially through three identical blocks. Each block consists of three stacked layers: a Conv layer (orange rectangle), a Norm layer (blue rectangle), and a ReLU layer (yellow rectangle), all contained within a green-bordered rectangular group. The output of each block is fed into a separate Style projector component, represented by a blue trapezoid labeled 'P'. Each Style projector produces a vertical orange bar labeled 'Style code', indicating a vector output. These three style codes are generated in parallel from the three feature extraction blocks.

The right section provides a detailed breakdown of the Style projector's internal architecture. It begins with a 'Feature' input, depicted as a stack of gray squares, which splits into two parallel branches. Each branch passes through a blue rectangular block labeled 'Max Pooling', producing sequences of small squares—yellow in the top branch and light green in the bottom branch. These sequences are then concatenated vertically into a single sequence of stacked yellow and green squares, labeled 'Concatenate'. This concatenated feature vector is processed by a series of layers: a Conv layer (orange rectangle), followed by three consecutive Linear layers (gray rectangles), and finally a Norm layer (blue rectangle). The output of the Norm layer is a horizontal orange bar labeled 'Style code', representing the final style code vector produced by the projector.

Connections between components are indicated by solid black arrows, showing the flow of data from input to output. The MSP module processes the image through multiple scales via its three sequential blocks, and each block’s output is independently projected into a style code using the same Style projector architecture. The Style projector itself uses max pooling to extract spatial features, concatenates them across channels, and then applies convolutional and fully connected layers to produce a normalized style code. The entire process is designed to generate multiple style codes from different feature scales, as described in the caption.

The figure is vertically split into two parts. The top section shows a 3D CNN-based hierarchical object proposal network, progressing from raw 3D input through multiple convolutional layers to generate Level 1 and Level 2 object proposals. The bottom section details the fine-tuning and classification pipeline, combining 3D features from a proposed region with 2D features extracted from a corresponding image patch using a pre-trained VGG network.

[2] Visual Modules and Attributes:
In the top section, the process begins with a purple rectangle labeled '3D Input', followed by a sequence of green rectangles ('Conv 1', 'Conv 2', 'Conv 3', 'Conv4') representing convolutional layers, and blue rectangles ('ReLU + Pool') indicating ReLU activation and pooling operations. After Conv 3, two parallel branches emerge: one leading to 'Conv Class' (green) followed by 'Softmax' (beige), and another to 'Conv 3D Box' (green) followed by 'L1 Smooth' (beige). These branches feed into Conv4, which repeats the same structure. Below this network, three 3D room visualizations show increasing levels of object proposal refinement: the first shows the full space (5.2×5.2×2.5 m³, receptive field 0.025³ m³), the second highlights Level 1 proposals (receptive field 0.4³ m³), and the third shows Level 2 proposals (receptive field 1.0³ m³), each with red wireframe bounding boxes.

From the 3D box, a path leads through green 'Conv 1', 'Conv 2', 'Conv 3' blocks and blue 'ReLU + Pool' blocks, then to a red 'FC 2' block. From the 2D image patch, a gray box labeled '2D VGG on ImageNet' feeds into a red 'FC 1' block. The outputs of FC 2 and FC 1 are concatenated via a tall red 'Concatenation' block, then passed through a red 'FC 3' block. From FC 3, two branches diverge: one to 'FC Class' (red) then 'Softmax' (beige), and another to 'FC 3D Box' (red) then 'L1 Smooth' (beige).

In the top section, arrows flow sequentially from '3D Input' through the convolutional and pooling layers. After Conv 3, two branches split: one to 'Conv Class' → 'Softmax', the other to 'Conv 3D Box' → 'L1 Smooth'. Both branches converge back into the main stream before Conv4, which repeats the branching pattern. Large downward-pointing white arrows connect the network outputs to the corresponding 3D visualization below, indicating the proposal generation at each level.

In the bottom section, arrows lead from the 3D box to the 3D CNN path (Conv 1 → ReLU+Pool → Conv 2 → ReLU+Pool → Conv 3 → ReLU → FC 2), and from the 2D image patch to the 2D VGG path (→ FC 1). Two arrows from FC 2 and FC 1 point to the 'Concatenation' block, which feeds into FC 3. From FC 3, two arrows branch out: one to 'FC Class' → 'Softmax', and the other to 'FC 3D Box' → 'L1 Smooth'. The figure illustrates the architecture of a multimodal model called \method-Swin, designed to process both video and audio inputs simultaneously. The global layout is vertically structured into three main sections: input processing at the bottom, a central encoder-decoder block repeated B times, and output heads at the top. The entire structure is organized to enable cross-modal interaction while preserving modality-specific representations.

At the bottom, two parallel input streams are shown: an input spectrogram of size 640×128 (audio) and an input video of dimensions 8×224×224×3 (video). These are processed via patching modules: 'Audio Patching' (teal box) converts the spectrogram into audio tokens of size 160×32×128, represented as a sequence of small teal squares. Similarly, 'Video Patching' (green box) processes the video into video tokens of size 8×56×56×128, depicted as small green squares. Both token sequences are then fed into position embedding (teal rectangular bar), which adds positional information.

The central part of the diagram consists of B identical blocks, outlined in orange and labeled with 'x B'. Within each block, the audio tokens (teal) pass through a '2D Swin Block', the video tokens (green) pass through a '3D Swin Block', and a separate set of fusion tokens (purple) are processed by 'Self-Attentions'. These three streams converge into a 'Cross Attention Module' (orange oval), where bidirectional arrows indicate that the fusion tokens attend to both audio and video tokens, enabling cross-modal interaction. The output from this module feeds back into the next iteration of the block, forming a recurrent-like structure across the B blocks.

Above the blocks, a gray bar labeled 'Decoding cross-attention' connects to four output heads: 'Audio Head' (teal), 'Fusion Head' (purple), 'Global Head' (purple), and 'Video Head' (green). Each head produces a 1×527 output vector, represented as stacked rectangles matching the color of the respective head. The diagram emphasizes that the decoding stage uses learned queries that cross-attend to the unimodal and multimodal representations, with masking applied to allow generation of both unimodal and multimodal outputs. This design ensures that unimodal representations depend only on their respective inputs, while fusion representations integrate both modalities. The architecture supports self-supervised training by enabling the model to generate outputs for each modality independently or jointly.

The figure illustrates the RRLD (Randomized Representation Learning with Distillation) framework, a method for training deep vision models using data augmentation and intermediate representation distillation. The global layout consists of two parallel processing streams: one for the original input x and another for its augmented version xa, both passing through a shared-weighted transformer-like network composed of sequential blocks b1, b2, ..., bn. The top stream processes the augmented input xa, while the bottom stream processes the original input x. Both streams share identical network weights, indicated by a double vertical bar labeled 'Shared Weights' between them.

In the visual modules, the input images are shown as 3x3 grids of patches, representing the tokenized input to the network. Each block bi (i=1 to n) is depicted as a light blue rectangle, symbolizing a transformer block or similar processing unit. At the end of each stream, the final block bn outputs a sequence of tokens: multiple white squares represent patch tokens, and a single dark blue square represents the class token. These tokens are fed into a green rectangular module labeled 'fc', denoting a fully connected layer that produces the final classification output. For the bottom stream, an additional 'fc' layer is applied to the output of a randomly selected intermediate block bi, producing bi(x), which is used for distillation loss.

Connections and arrows indicate the data flow and training signals. Black arrows show forward propagation: from input x and xa to the respective block sequences, and from the final class token to the fc layers. In the bottom stream, orange arrows point backward from later blocks to earlier ones, labeled 'Backpropagation' in the legend, indicating gradient flow during training. A gray box labeled 'Intermediate Block Selection' receives outputs from all blocks in the bottom stream and selects one at random to extract bi(x). The outputs bn(xa), bn(x), and bi(x) are used to compute three distinct losses: La (augmentation loss) between bn(xa) and bn(x), Lce (cross-entropy loss) for the final prediction bn(x), and Li (intermediate loss) between bi(x) and bn(x). These losses are combined to train the model. The legend clarifies that white squares are patch tokens, dark blue squares are class tokens, and orange arrows denote backpropagation. The figure caption explains that AutoAugment transforms x into xa, and gradient computation is halted for the augmented path during training, as per Algorithm ref{alg:label}.

The figure presents an overview of the Denoising Fusion Bottleneck (DBF) model, designed for multimodal learning involving visual/audio and textual inputs. The global layout is structured as a hierarchical pipeline enclosed within a dashed rectangular boundary, representing the core model architecture. At the bottom, two distinct input streams are shown: 'Visual/Audio Input' on the left and 'Textual Input' on the right. Each stream feeds into a separate stack of N Transformer Layers, depicted as beige rounded rectangles, which serve as initial encoders for each modality. These encoder outputs are represented as sequences of embeddings: light gray cubes for regular tokens and a yellow cube labeled '[CLS]' at the beginning of each sequence, indicating the classification token. A legend on the top-right clarifies that yellow cubes denote [CLS] Embedding and green cubes denote Bottleneck Embeddings.

Above the initial encoders, the model transitions into a fusion stage consisting of M Transformer Layers, also shown as beige rounded rectangles. These layers receive inputs from both modalities and are interconnected via bidirectional arrows, suggesting cross-modal attention or interaction. Between these M layers, a green cube labeled 'Bottleneck Embeddings' is inserted, indicating a compact representation extracted during fusion. The outputs of the M Transformer Layers are then processed by two MI-Max modules, one on each side, which are beige rounded rectangles connected to the respective modality’s output sequence. These MI-Max modules extract features for contrastive learning.

From the MI-Max modules, two paths emerge: a 'Positive' path connects the two MI-Max outputs to an 'InfoNCE Loss' block, while a 'Negative' path connects to 'In-batch Negatives', represented as multiple light gray cubes. This setup implements a contrastive loss function to maximize mutual information between modalities. Additionally, the fused representations from the M Transformer Layers are averaged and passed through 'Output Layers', a beige rounded rectangle, which then feed into a 'Task Loss' block at the top, indicating the final supervised objective.

The diagram uses solid black arrows to indicate data flow and dashed lines to denote structural grouping or iterative processes (e.g., M × and N ×). The color coding is consistent: beige for processing layers, gray for loss components, yellow for [CLS] tokens, and green for bottleneck embeddings. The overall structure reflects a dual-encoder, multi-layer fusion framework with explicit contrastive regularization via MI-Max and InfoNCE loss, aimed at preserving critical information during multimodal integration.

The figure presents a five-step process for establishing construct validity of psychometric tests administered to large language models (LLMs). The layout is divided into five main sections arranged in a 2x3 grid, with steps 1 and 2 on the top row, steps 3 and 4 on the middle row, and step 5 at the bottom right. Step 1, titled 'Administer Psychometric Tests,' is a simple rectangular box indicating the initial action of giving LLMs personality assessments. Step 2, 'Evaluate Reliability,' contains three parallelogram-shaped nodes labeled 'Cronbach's Alpha,' 'Guttman's Lambda 6,' and 'McDonald's Omega,' which feed into a diamond-shaped decision node asking if all reliability metrics are ≥ 0.70. If yes, a blue rounded rectangle labeled 'Reliability' is reached. Step 3, 'Evaluate Convergent & Discriminant Validity,' shows stacked document icons representing 'IPIP-NEO Subscales' and 'BFI Subscales,' connected by an arrow to a small square labeled 'rs' (correlation coefficient), which feeds into a diamond-shaped decision node asking if convergent rs ≥ 0.80. A 'Yes' path leads to a magenta rounded rectangle labeled 'Convergent Validity.' From this, another arrow leads to a second diamond node asking if the average convergent rs minus average discriminant rs is ≥ 0.40; a 'Yes' path leads to a yellow rounded rectangle labeled 'Discriminant Validity.' Step 4, 'Evaluate Criterion Validity,' displays two rows: the top row contains five document-shaped nodes labeled 'IPIP-NEO EXT,' 'AGR,' 'CON,' 'NEU,' 'OPE,' grouped under 'IPIP-NEO Subscales'; the bottom row contains five similar nodes labeled 'Pos. Affect,' 'Aggression,' 'Achievement Values,' 'Neg. Affect,' 'Creativity,' grouped under 'External Criteria.' These are linked via arrows to a central 'r' node, which connects to a diamond-shaped decision node asking if criterion rs align with human data. A 'Yes' path leads to a purple rounded rectangle labeled 'Criterion Validity.' Step 5, 'Judge Construct Validity,' features four colored rounded rectangles—magenta ('Convergent Validity'), yellow ('Discriminant Validity'), blue ('Reliability'), and purple ('Criterion Validity')—each pointing to a central pentagon labeled 'Construct Validity,' indicating that all four components contribute to the final judgment. All connections are represented by solid black arrows, and the entire process is designed to assess the psychometric properties of LLM-generated personality test responses, based on resampled data from 1,250 trials with varied biographic descriptions and item instructions.

The figure presents a knowledge distillation framework for GAN compression, structured as a flowchart with distinct modules and directional connections. The global layout is horizontal, progressing from left to right, with two parallel pathways: a teacher model and a student model, both receiving the same input. Below these pathways, a separate sequence of MCMC sampling steps is shown, feeding into the final energy-based model. The top-right corner contains a legend indicating red arrows mean 'Minimize', blue arrows mean 'Maximize', and a circle with a plus sign denotes 'Concatenate'.

The visual modules are represented by trapezoidal shapes for encoders and decoders, rectangular boxes for outputs and intermediate states, and a large pink trapezoid for the final energy-based model. The teacher encoder is yellow, the teacher decoder is light blue, the student encoder is orange, and the student decoder is dark blue. All text within modules is black and centered. The input box is white, and the MCMC state boxes (t^0, ..., t^K) are green. The teacher and student encoders are connected vertically by a gray arrow labeled 'Knowledge Distillation', indicating the transfer of knowledge from teacher to student.

The workflow begins with the 'Input' box, which feeds into both the 'Teacher Encoder' and 'Student Encoder'. The teacher encoder outputs to the 'Teacher Decoder', which then produces 'Teacher Output'. Similarly, the student encoder connects to the 'Student Decoder', producing 'Student Output'. The teacher output and student output are both directed toward the 'Energy-based Model' via concatenation operations (indicated by ⊕ symbols). Specifically, the teacher output is concatenated with the student output using a red arrow (minimize), and the student output is also concatenated with the MCMC sample t^K using a blue arrow (maximize). These concatenated inputs feed into the 'Energy-based Model', which is the final component in the pipeline.

Below the main pathway, the 'Student Output' is used to initialize a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) process. This starts at state t^0, which is passed through successive 'Run MCMC' steps, leading to t^K after K iterations. The final MCMC state t^K is then concatenated with the student output (via the blue 'Maximize' arrow) before being fed into the energy-based model. The entire framework aims to maximize the variational lower bound of mutual information between the teacher and student models, leveraging the energy-based model to guide the distillation process through minimization and maximization objectives.

The figure presents an overview of the Autoregressive Motion Diffusion (AMD) model, structured into three main vertical sections: two identical 'Context Encoder' blocks on the left and right, flanking a central green-colored 'AMD Module' section. The global layout is horizontal and sequential, illustrating an iterative autoregressive process where each step generates motion conditioned on previous text and motion inputs.

In the left 'Context Encoder' block (light blue background), three inputs are processed: the current text prompt S^i (blue dashed arrow), the previous text prompt S^{i-1} (green arrow), and the previous motion X_0^{i-1} (green arrow). These inputs are fed into distinct modules: S^i goes through an encoder E_D (rounded rectangle, blue border); S^{i-1} passes through E_S (trapezoid, blue border); and X_0^{i-1} is processed by a 'Motion Linear' module (rounded rectangle, blue border). All three outputs converge into a circular node labeled 'T', which feeds into the central AMD module. Additionally, S^i is also directly connected via a dashed blue arrow to E_D, suggesting a parallel processing path.

The central green section represents the AMD module. It receives two inputs: the corrupted motion X_T^i (green downward arrow) and the contextual embedding T from the left encoder. Inside this module, a large rounded rectangle labeled 'AMD' processes these inputs to produce the cleaned motion X_0^i (green downward arrow). Below the AMD box, a sequence of 10 stylized human figures in various poses visually represents the generated motion sequence, emphasizing the output's nature as human motion data.

The right 'Context Encoder' block mirrors the left one but operates at the next time step. It receives S^{i+1} (blue dashed arrow), S^i (green arrow), and X_0^i (green arrow) as inputs. These are processed similarly: S^{i+1} through E_D, S^i through E_S, and X_0^i through 'Motion Linear'. Their outputs again converge into a 'T' node, which feeds into the next iteration (not shown). A key connection from the central AMD module shows X_0^i being combined with S^i via a circular summation node (with a '+' symbol), producing a green arrow that feeds into the right encoder’s E_S module, indicating that the generated motion is used as context for the next step.

Connections are color-coded: green arrows represent motion or state data flow (e.g., X_0^{i-1}, X_0^i), while blue arrows denote text prompt or latent representation flow (e.g., S^i, S^{i-1}). Dashed blue arrows indicate auxiliary or optional paths. The figure emphasizes an iterative pipeline where each step uses the previous step’s output to condition the next, enabling generation of long motion sequences from extended text prompts.

The figure illustrates the architecture and training pipeline of the Deep Operator Energy Method based on the Principle of Minimum Complementary Energy (DCEM-O). The global layout is structured into two main vertical columns: the left column contains four neural network components receiving inputs, and the right column contains loss functions and optimization stages. The workflow proceeds from left to right, with a clear two-stage optimization process.

On the left side, the top three networks—Particular Net θ_p, Basis Net θ_b, and Trunk Net θ_T—are depicted as identical multi-layer feedforward neural networks, each represented by a rectangular box containing blue circular nodes connected by lines to form a fully connected structure. Each network outputs a set of purple circular nodes labeled p_i through p_m. These three networks receive input data x_1 through x_m, indicated by blue circles with an orange curved arrow looping from the input to each network. Each of these networks is pre-trained independently, as denoted by the 'Pretrain' label next to each.

Below these, the Branch Net θ_B is shown as a stacked block diagram with light blue rectangular layers labeled FNN, CNN, RNN, and Transformer..., indicating a modular design capable of integrating various neural architectures. This net receives physical parameters such as Geometry, Material, Force, etc., as input, indicated by a pink arrow pointing to it.

In the center, the outputs of the Particular Net and Basis Net are combined via a summation operation (represented by a circle with a plus sign), while the outputs of the Trunk Net and Branch Net are combined via a multiplication operation (represented by a circle with a dot). The result of the summation is fed into the Stress function, which is a yellow rectangular box. The Stress function then feeds into the Data loss, a magenta rectangular box, with an arrow labeled 'Optimize First', indicating this is the first stage of optimization.

The output of the multiplication operation is fed into the Complementary energy, a teal rectangular box. An arrow labeled 'Minimize θ_T θ_B' points from the Complementary energy back to the Trunk Net and Branch Net, indicating that these two networks are optimized together in the second stage, labeled 'Optimize Second'.

The overall structure emphasizes a two-phase training strategy: first, pretraining the Particular and Basis Nets and optimizing the Stress function to minimize Data loss; second, minimizing the Complementary energy by jointly optimizing the Trunk and Branch Nets. The diagram uses distinct colors for different functional blocks (magenta for Data loss, yellow for Stress function, teal for Complementary energy) and clear directional arrows to indicate data flow and optimization sequence.
